text: Solara AI built solara-train's inter-node fabric on InfiniBand NDR instead of Ethernet. This lesson explains that choice concretely, with real numbers instead of vague preference.

The headline difference isn't raw bandwidth — modern Ethernet can match InfiniBand's four hundred gigabit port speed. It's latency and loss behavior. InfiniBand NDR runs at roughly one microsecond or less, switch to switch, and it's natively lossless. Ethernet with RoCEv2 can get close, in the low microseconds, but it takes careful tuning of priority flow control and ECN to get there, and it's easier to get that tuning wrong than it is on InfiniBand. Plain Ethernet TCP/IP, without any of that, runs tens of microseconds or more, and handles loss through retransmission.

That matters because of GPUDirect RDMA — letting a network adapter write straight into or out of GPU memory, skipping the CPU and the operating system's network stack entirely. NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL controls how aggressively that happens, and InfiniBand has supported it natively for years.

Here's why losslessness specifically matters for collectives. InfiniBand uses credit-based flow control — a sender only transmits once the receiver has confirmed it has buffer space, so packets essentially never drop from congestion. Plain TCP/IP instead drops packets and retransmits, and because a ring AllReduce is fully synchronous, one dropped packet stalls every single GPU in the ring until it's resent.

InfiniBand's real edge is sub-microsecond latency and a natively lossless fabric — not raw bandwidth. That's not to say Ethernet is never the right call, just that collective-heavy LLM training, with its constant small synchronous messages, is close to the worst case for its weaknesses. Up next, lesson ten: how that InfiniBand fabric actually gets wired into a cluster-wide topology.
